strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: interpretable error-slice discovery for instance-level detection and segmentation, where spatial and relational context cannot be represented adequately by image-level clusters or simple attribute conjunctions.

GH-ESD is conceptually coherent: it combines knowledge- and data-driven hypothesis generation, region-conditioned VLM matching, and subsequent verification. Natural-language relational hypotheses are more expressive and actionable than atomic tags.

GESD could be a valuable benchmark contribution. It covers over 12K images from multiple public datasets, aggregates failures from several model families, and reportedly involves 1,500 person-hours of annotation for 42 spatially grounded slices.

The reported detection results are promising: GH-ESD improves P@10 from 0.63 to 0.73 over the strongest HiBug2 variant and leads at P@5 and P@20. Using the same Gemini backend for HiBug2 helps separate framework improvements from LLM choice.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond the headline comparison, including FP/FN and category breakdowns, knowledge- versus data-driven hypotheses, image- versus instance-level grounding, an alternative Spearman test, classical bias benchmarks, and downstream model-repair experiments.

The presentation is generally clear, with an intuitive overview and concrete qualitative examples. The limitations concerning dataset coverage and incomplete hypothesis spaces are appropriately acknowledged.
weaknesses: The primary statistical verification rule does not justify its stated interpretation. Defining Trend(h) as the maximum slope over sliding windows does not test a consistent monotonic increase; a hypothesis can pass because of one favorable local window despite flat or negative behavior elsewhere. Maximization over many overlapping windows and generated hypotheses also creates substantial selection bias, yet the primary method provides neither a null calibration nor multiple-testing control. The Spearman/FDR variant is more defensible but is only reported as a secondary aggregate result.

The main Precision@k evaluation protocol is underspecified and potentially optimistic. It is unclear exactly how many-to-many predicted and ground-truth slices are matched, whether the best predicted slice is selected separately for each ground-truth slice, and how unmatched or redundant hypotheses are penalized. P@k alone primarily measures retrieval purity and does not establish slice coverage; the separate hypothesis precision/recall analysis relies on an LLM semantic judge rather than independent human assessment.

There is a risk of circularity in GESD: experts define slices after inspecting the aggregated errors, while the method generates and verifies hypotheses on the same benchmark. The manuscript does not describe a held-out hypothesis-discovery/test split or evaluation on independently defined slices. Moreover, replacing every non-slice prediction with ground truth produces a synthetic closed-world benchmark that may exaggerate performance and complicates evaluation of newly discovered, unannotated failure modes.

The comparison does not adequately isolate all components. Only one fixed hypothesis is used to support the benefit of instance-level grounding, and the reported KD/DD numbers are not a controlled full factorial ablation. Several baselines require substantial adaptations, while the relevant VISLIX method is discussed but not evaluated. Results lack uncertainty estimates or significance tests for the principal P@k comparisons.

Evidence for broader claims is incomplete in the supplied manuscript. Segmentation performance is deferred entirely to supplementary material, despite cross-task support being a central claim. Dataset slice statistics, annotation agreement, matching guidelines, per-dataset/model results, sensitivity to alternative LLM/VLM backends, prompts, and important implementation details are likewise absent from the provided document.

The repair study does not establish that gains come specifically from correctly discovered slices: GroupDRO plus GH-ESD is compared with ordinary fine-tuning, but not with GroupDRO using random groups, model-error scores, or oracle slices. The evaluation set and possible overlap with the COCO validation data used during discovery are unclear, and overall detection performance or regressions on other classes are not reported.

Reproducibility is limited by dependence on proprietary Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-5.2 services without reported prompts in the main paper, decoding settings, API versions, cost, runtime, or variability across repeated generation. The central matching-score equation is also visibly malformed in the PDF. Overall, evaluated under the default Algorithms/General type while recognizing the substantial benchmark component, the idea is promising but the statistical and evaluation issues leave a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: interpretable, instance-level failure discovery for detection and segmentation, especially failures involving spatial context and object relationships.

The combination of top-down LLM hypotheses, bottom-up grounded descriptions, VLM-based instance matching, and subsequent verification is intuitive and produces human-readable slices. The reported GESD detection results improve Precision@10 from 0.63 to 0.73 over HiBug2.

GESD could be a useful community resource: it covers more than 12K images, errors from four detectors and one segmentation model, 42 expert-defined hypotheses, and reportedly substantial manual annotation effort.

The paper evaluates several aspects beyond its principal detection experiment, including component comparisons, image-classification bias benchmarks, false-positive/false-negative breakdowns, and downstream model repair. It also acknowledges incomplete hypothesis coverage and dataset dependence as limitations.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction is fundamentally circular. Experts define slices after examining errors from the same models and datasets, and all predictions outside those predefined slices are overwritten with ground truth. This produces a synthetic closed world in which only the selected hypotheses can explain errors, suppressing unknown errors and false discoveries. Consequently, the benchmark does not convincingly measure open-ended slice discovery under realistic model outputs.

The principal Precision@k evaluation is underspecified and inadequate for the discovery claim. Equation (1) scores a given predicted/ground-truth slice pair, but the paper does not clearly specify the pairing or aggregation procedure when predicted and ground-truth slices split or merge. Precision@k alone largely measures instance retrieval after a compatible hypothesis exists; it does not measure whether important slices are discovered, whether hypotheses are redundant, or how many false hypotheses are returned.

The proposed statistical verification does not justify its claims. Taking the maximum regression slope over sliding windows is not a test of an overall monotonic relationship: one noisy local fluctuation can make a hypothesis pass. Window size and stride are unspecified, the slope depends on VLM-score scaling, windows may contain as few as five samples, and the main variant has neither a significance test nor multiple-comparison correction. The Spearman/FDR alternative is mentioned only through a single aggregate result and does not validate the default procedure.

Several evaluations introduce circularity or evaluator bias. Hypothesis precision and recall are judged by Gemini-2.5-Pro, which is also the method's hypothesis-generation backend, using an unspecified semantic-relatedness criterion. This automatic judge may favor similarly phrased language hypotheses over atomic-tag baselines; no blinded human evaluation, judge agreement, or sensitivity to alternative judges is reported.

Baseline fairness is weak. FACTS is reduced to image-level error labels, while HiBug methods are modified and run with new proprietary LLMs. The main comparison therefore mixes methods, adaptation choices, language backends, and grounding capabilities. Missing controls include direct natural-language hypothesis retrieval without the proposed verification, identical VLM grounding applied to baseline hypotheses, and oracle/manual hypotheses to separate generation from retrieval.

The ablations do not isolate the claimed components convincingly. Instance- versus image-level grounding is tested on only one fixed hypothesis; knowledge-driven and data-driven variants are reported only as isolated P@10 numbers; and verification is compared using aggregate F1 without counts, uncertainty, per-slice results, or independent repetitions. Main GESD results also lack confidence intervals or variability across stochastic LLM/VLM runs.

The segmentation contribution is not adequately supported in the supplied manuscript. It relies on one Mask R-CNN and refers the only quantitative results to an unavailable supplementary table. More broadly, crucial prompts, complete slice definitions and statistics, matching details, parameter calibration, and repair protocols are deferred to supplementary material that is not present, substantially limiting reproducibility and verification.

The dataset documentation is insufficient for a benchmark contribution. It gives no per-slice sample counts in the main paper, annotator recruitment details, independent labeling protocol, inter-annotator agreement, adjudication statistics, class/model coverage, leakage analysis, or concrete release and licensing plan. The phrase 'every relevant instance' also leaves unclear how candidate instances were selected and whether unlabeled positives were missed.

The model-repair experiment does not establish that the discovered slices cause the gains. GH-ESD is combined with GroupDRO, but there are no GroupDRO controls using random groups, generic hard-example mining, ground-truth slices, or HiBug2 slices. The evaluation split is also unclear; because GESD includes COCO validation images used to select the bicycle hypothesis, reporting repair performance on overlapping validation data would create selection leakage.

Overall, the paper presents a promising formulation, but the circular benchmark, incomplete discovery metric, statistically questionable verification rule, and insufficiently controlled experiments undermine the central scientific claims. I assess it primarily as Algorithms/General with a substantial Datasets/Benchmarks component; neither component is yet supported strongly enough for acceptance.

strengths: The central reframing—instance-level slice discovery as grounded natural-language hypothesis generation followed by verification—is well motivated for detection and segmentation, where relational and spatial failures are poorly represented by image-level clusters or atomic tags.

GH-ESD coherently combines top-down knowledge-driven and bottom-up dataset-driven hypotheses, grounds them to regions using continuous VLM scores, and produces interpretable failure descriptions. The reported complementarity of the two hypothesis sources supports this design.

GESD addresses an important benchmarking gap. It uses more than 12K images from three domains, errors from four detectors and one segmentation model, 42 expert-defined grounded hypotheses, and substantial instance-level human annotation.

The detection results are promising: GH-ESD improves P@10 from 0.63 to 0.73 over the strongest HiBug2 variant, leads at P@5 and P@20, and improves both false-positive and false-negative slices. Matching HiBug2's Gemini backend is a useful control against attributing the gain solely to model choice.

The paper includes useful component analyses and evidence beyond retrieval: instance grounding improves the examined slice, trend verification improves F1 over error-rate thresholding, results transfer to image-level bias benchmarks, and slice-aware repair substantially raises bicycle mAP/mAR. The presentation is generally clear, and limitations concerning incomplete hypothesis coverage are appropriately acknowledged.
weaknesses: The benchmark metric and slice-matching protocol are underspecified. Equation (1) defines precision for one ground-truth/predicted-slice pair, but the paper does not clearly explain pair selection under splits and merges or aggregation across slices. An oracle best-match procedure could materially inflate P@k; the evaluation should also penalize duplicate, redundant, or excessive predictions.

The default verifier does not establish the claimed “consistent monotonic” relationship: it takes the maximum slope across sliding windows, so one favorable local window can validate an otherwise flat or contradictory hypothesis. This introduces implicit multiple testing, while window width, stride, and slope uncertainty are not specified. The Spearman/FDR variant is reassuring but should be evaluated on the main GESD retrieval results and considered as the default.

Hypothesis quality is partly judged by Gemini-2.5-Pro, also used to construct GH-ESD hypotheses. This creates a risk of evaluator self-preference, especially when comparing fluent hypotheses with terse tag combinations. Blinded human evaluation, inter-rater agreement, or an independent matching protocol would strengthen the reported precision/recall comparison.

The main GESD comparison lacks uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, significance tests, and detailed per-slice results. GESD is constructed from errors of the evaluated model families and overwrites non-slice predictions with ground truth, yielding a partly synthetic closed-world evaluation. Cross-model holdouts would better demonstrate generalization and reduce benchmark/model circularity.

Important evidence is deferred to a supplement absent from the supplied manuscript, including full slice statistics, prompts, model-sensitivity experiments, segmentation results, baseline adaptations, and repair settings. Thus, segmentation support and reproducibility cannot be adequately assessed. Dependence on changing proprietary APIs also calls for model snapshots, costs, seeds, and run-to-run variability.

Several baselines were designed for classification and undergo lossy image-level adaptation, making their weak results unsurprising. Stronger controlled comparisons should isolate the effects of relational hypotheses, region grounding, and statistical filtering under identical candidate budgets and VLM calls; the current single-hypothesis grounding ablation is too narrow.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: interpretable error-slice discovery for instance-level detection and segmentation, where spatial and relational conditions cannot be represented adequately by image-level clusters or independent tags.

GH-ESD is a coherent generate-and-verify framework. Natural-language hypotheses, region-conditioned VLM matching, and continuous match scores are sensible ingredients for discovering contextual failures such as occlusion by another object or visual confusion between object types.

GESD is potentially valuable: it covers more than 12K images, detection and segmentation, 42 expert-defined slices, several model families, and reportedly required 1,500 person-hours of annotation. The per-slice statistics and examples make the intended benchmark content relatively concrete.

The experimental scope is broad, including detection, segmentation, established image-level bias datasets, component analyses, alternative LLM/VLM backends, efficiency measurements, and downstream repair experiments.

The manuscript is generally clear and supplies prompts, per-slice results, and many implementation details. I assess it primarily as Algorithms/General, while recognizing GESD as a substantial Datasets/Benchmarks contribution.
weaknesses: The main GESD evaluation has serious circularity and construct-validity concerns. Experts define the ground-truth slices by inspecting an aggregated pool of model errors, and predictions outside those predefined slices are then overwritten with ground truth. The resulting benchmark measures recovery of a curated, closed set of known failures rather than realistic open-ended slice discovery. There is no convincing evaluation on held-out datasets, model families, or independently defined failures that would establish generalization beyond this construction process.

The principal Precision@k protocol is insufficiently defined and appears oracle-assisted. Supplementary Tables S3 and S4 report the "Best Predicted Slice" separately for every ground-truth slice, but the paper does not specify a non-oracle matching and ranking procedure. Selecting the best among many generated hypotheses using ground-truth membership can inflate results, does not penalize redundant or spurious discovered slices, and does not reflect what a practitioner would receive from the method. The separate semantic precision/recall analysis relies on an LLM judge rather than blinded human evaluation.

The proposed statistical verification is not statistically justified. Taking the maximum slope over multiple sliding windows—some containing as few as five samples—does not demonstrate a "consistent monotonic" relationship; it actively selects the most favorable local fluctuation and introduces an uncorrected multiple-comparison problem. Window size and stride are unspecified, confidence calibration for gamma is not documented, and candidate generation and verification apparently use the same data. The Spearman/FDR variant is encouraging but is reported only through aggregate F1 and does not repair the validity of the main test.

Evidence for the claimed advantage over prior work is not sufficiently controlled. FACTS is reduced to image-level aggregation, HiBug is adapted using an interactively constructed attribute corpus, and the compared systems have substantially different candidate spaces and model dependencies. Table 1 provides no repeated-run uncertainty, statistical test, or analysis of sensitivity to candidate count. The ablations are mostly isolated examples or indirect comparisons rather than a complete controlled decomposition on GESD.

Benchmark reproducibility and annotation quality are underdocumented. The manuscript gives no inter-annotator agreement, adjudication statistics, precise annotation guidelines, benchmark split, or evaluation implementation. Important details such as the number of sampled images for data-driven hypothesis construction, detector checkpoints and error-matching thresholds, sliding-window settings, and exact predicted-to-ground-truth slice matching are missing. The abstract's public-release URL is blank, and licensing/privacy considerations for the constituent datasets—particularly the face dataset—are not discussed.

The repair study does not isolate the value of slice discovery. GH-ESD is paired with GroupDRO and different optimization settings, while the baseline is ordinary fine-tuning; random, oracle, and alternative-slice GroupDRO controls are absent. For classification, LADDER is evaluated with its native ensemble whereas other methods use a different DFR protocol, limiting direct comparability. Thus the repair gains cannot confidently be attributed to better discovered slices.

Overall, the idea and dataset effort are promising, but the oracle-like evaluation, benchmark circularity, and invalid main trend statistic are consequential shortcomings. These affect the central empirical case rather than being presentation-level corrections.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: interpretable error-slice discovery for instance-level tasks, where spatial and relational conditions are not well represented by image-level clusters or atomic tags.

The grounded natural-language hypothesis formulation is intuitive and potentially useful. Combining top-down LLM priors, data-driven descriptions, region-conditioned VLM scoring, and downstream verification forms a coherent debugging workflow.

GESD represents substantial annotation effort across more than 12K images, multiple detectors, and both detection and segmentation. The per-slice statistics and detailed qualitative descriptions are valuable starting points for benchmark development.

The evaluation is broad, covering detection, segmentation, image-level bias benchmarks, component analyses, and model repair. The manuscript and supplementary material are generally clear and provide the main prompts and numerous slice-level results.
weaknesses: The primary GESD evaluation does not convincingly measure slice discovery. Precision@k is reported separately for every ground-truth slice using its "best predicted slice," apparently selecting retrospectively among generated hypotheses. This oracle-style matching, without a fully specified assignment protocol or penalty for missed, redundant, or spurious discoveries, can substantially inflate performance. The main metric therefore measures retrieval after alignment more than autonomous discovery.

GESD is highly constructed and potentially circular. Experts define 42 slices after examining aggregated model errors, and all predictions outside those predefined slices are overwritten with ground truth. This removes unknown real errors and creates an artificially closed benchmark that favors recovery of the curated taxonomy. The paper consequently overstates evaluation on realistic, open-ended failure discovery.

The proposed statistical verification is technically questionable. Taking the maximum regression slope over sliding windows neither establishes a global monotonic trend nor controls selection bias; a single small window, potentially containing only five samples, can pass the test. The statistic also depends on score calibration and window definition, yet the exact window sizes and calibration procedure are missing. Calling this reliable statistical verification is unsupported. The Spearman/FDR variant is only briefly reported and does not repair the primary evaluation.

The method and evaluation reuse the same data: data-driven hypotheses are generated from the target dataset, verified on its errors, and then evaluated against slices derived from those same errors. There is no held-out slice-definition or verification split demonstrating that hypotheses generalize beyond the data used to construct and select them.

Baseline evidence is insufficient and potentially unfair. Only three adapted baselines are evaluated on GESD, VISLIX is omitted, and the adaptations reduce some methods to image-level errors. Matching HiBug2's Gemini backend controls only part of a pipeline in which GH-ESD also uses Qwen2.5-VL. The semantic precision/recall comparison additionally relies on a single LLM judge and compares methods producing very different numbers of candidates (102 versus 3,666), without human validation or judge-agreement analysis.

The model-repair experiment does not isolate the value of discovered slices. The ordinary fine-tuning baseline uses a learning rate of 1e-5, whereas GroupDRO+GH-ESD uses 5e-5; thus the large gain cannot be attributed to slice-aware weighting. There is no GroupDRO control using random, generic, or ground-truth groups, and evaluation is restricted to one bicycle hypothesis. The stated 10-epoch schedule also includes a milestone at epoch 11.

Dataset quality and reproducibility documentation are inadequate for a benchmark contribution. The paper reports collaborative expert definition but no independent annotation protocol, inter-annotator agreement, adjudication statistics, or per-source/model breakdown. Important implementation details such as sampled-image counts, sliding-window configuration, detector checkpoints and thresholds, exact target model used in each benchmark evaluation, and full computational cost are absent. The abstract also states that GESD is publicly available but provides no URL.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence: the paper attributes gains to grounding and statistical verification despite mostly one-factor or single-hypothesis analyses, describes the tool as production-ready without deployment evaluation, and claims defensible slice identification despite the invalid maximum-window test. These are central scientific issues rather than minor presentation corrections.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: interpretable error-slice discovery for instance-level vision tasks, where spatial, contextual, and relational failure patterns are poorly captured by conventional embedding clusters or atomic attribute combinations.

GH-ESD is a coherent and reasonably original generate-and-verify framework. Combining LLM-based hypothesis construction, region-grounded VLM matching, and trend-based verification is technically intuitive and produces human-readable failure descriptions.

GESD is a valuable additional contribution. It covers more than 12K images from COCO, KITTI, and a face dataset; includes detection and segmentation errors from multiple model families; and provides 42 expert-defined, spatially grounded slices backed by a reported 1,500 person-hours of annotation.

The main detection results are encouraging and consistent across retrieval depths: GH-ESD obtains P@5/P@10/P@20 of 0.78/0.73/0.66, compared with 0.73/0.63/0.53 for the strongest GPT-based HiBug2 baseline. Using Gemini for HiBug2 as well helps separate the method improvement from the language-model backend.

The ablations support the main design choices. Language hypotheses are substantially more compact than HiBug2's tag combinations, instance grounding improves P@10 from 0.60 to 0.80 in the controlled example, and trend verification modestly improves F1 and threshold robustness. The Spearman variant with significance testing and FDR correction is a useful robustness check.

The method transfers well to the image-level Waterbirds, CelebA, and NICO++ benchmarks, while the detailed segmentation evaluation reaches mean P@10 of 0.805 across 21 slices. These results suggest that the approach is not restricted to one dataset or task.

The model-repair experiments provide evidence of practical value: slice-aware GroupDRO raises bicycle mAP from 28.58 to 33.59 over ordinary fine-tuning, and GH-ESD attains competitive worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds and CelebA.

The manuscript is clearly organized, visually polished, and unusually complete in its supplementary material, which includes prompts, per-slice results, implementation details, efficiency comparisons, and an interactive analysis tool. As no contribution type is declared, I assess it as Algorithms/General, while recognizing GESD as a substantial benchmark contribution.
weaknesses: The primary metric gives an incomplete picture of end-to-end slice discovery. Each ground-truth slice is paired with its best predicted slice and evaluated by Precision@k, which requires oracle ground-truth matching, does not measure how well the system ranks discovered hypotheses, and does not penalize unsupported discoveries. The LLM-based hypothesis precision/recall analysis partly addresses this issue, but it relies on a single automated semantic evaluator rather than independent human judgments.

The benchmark is deliberately curated rather than a faithful natural error distribution: experts select slices from pooled model failures, and predictions outside those predefined slices are overwritten with ground truth. This isolates the annotated patterns but removes unknown errors and may inflate apparent discovery quality. Evaluation on untouched real model outputs, ideally with held-out models and datasets not involved in slice construction, would better support claims of general deployment utility.

The main slope statistic is not a convincing monotonicity test. Taking the maximum local regression slope over sliding windows can retain a hypothesis because of one small increasing region even when the global relationship is inconsistent, and searching over windows and hypotheses introduces selection effects. The Spearman test with significance testing and FDR correction is methodologically stronger and should arguably be the primary procedure rather than a supplementary variant.

The segmentation evidence lacks comparisons against adapted competing methods, despite the paper's cross-task claims. Reporting only GH-ESD's per-slice P@10 demonstrates feasibility but not superiority for segmentation.

GESD's annotation protocol needs stronger reliability reporting. The three researchers collaboratively define the slices, but the paper provides no independent annotation agreement, adjudication statistics, or evaluation of slice-definition ambiguity. This matters because several ground-truth and predicted descriptions are only approximate semantic matches.

The model-repair comparison is confounded by different optimization settings: ordinary fine-tuning uses a learning rate of 1e-5, whereas GroupDRO uses 5e-5. Only bicycle-class mAP/mAR are reported, so it is also unclear whether the targeted repair harms other categories or improves performance specifically within the discovered slice.

Reproducibility is limited by reliance on proprietary Gemini and GPT backends, the absence of some operational details such as the number and selection of images used for data-driven hypothesis construction, and the missing public dataset URL in the supplied manuscript. Total end-to-end compute and scaling cost across all hypotheses and instances are also not reported.

Overall, these concerns limit the strength of the empirical conclusions but do not outweigh the paper's clear novelty, useful benchmark, broad evaluation, and practical relevance. The contribution supports acceptance with reservations.
